draft.title: Bounded self-interest
card: Bounded self-interest means people do not look after only their own gain. They also care about fairness and about other people.
This is why people donate to charity, leave a tip, or help a stranger, even when it costs them and brings no money back.
People may also refuse an offer they think is unfair, even if accepting would leave them better off than saying no.
Traditional economics assumes people act to benefit only themselves. Bounded self-interest shows that fairness and concern for others also shape choices.
draft.remember: Bounded self-interest: people sometimes give up their own gain because they care about fairness or others.

a.q: Sam in Bendigo is offered $2 from a $20 prize that a partner shared out. Sam says no, even though $2 is better than nothing. What best explains this?
opts: He sees the split as unfair and cares about fairness
He did not have time to think about the offer
He was unable to resist spending the money now
He wants to earn as much money as he can
a.why: Refusing free money costs Sam $2, so it is not about his own gain. He acts on fairness, which is bounded self-interest. Wanting the most money would lead him to accept.
a.clue: Accepting would have left him better off.

b.q: A group of friends in Mildura raise $400 for a flood relief charity. They get nothing back. Which idea does this show?
opts: Bounded self-interest, as they care about others
Bounded willpower, as they chose the present over later
Bounded rationality, as they had too little information
Traditional economics, as they act only for personal gain
b.why: The friends give up money to help others, so they do not act only for themselves. That is bounded self-interest. Traditional economics assumes self-interest, so it does not fit.
b.clue: Who gains from the money the friends gave?

a.best: He sees the split as unfair and cares about fairness

b.best: Bounded self-interest, as they care about others
